title: Robust game theory
contribution: Defines robust games, in which players maximize worst-case expected payoff over a commonly known payoff uncertainty set, proves their equilibria exist and contain the ex post equilibria, and computes them through an LP-duality multilinear system.
problem_entry: {RO+LO} Bayesian games need a common prior and the distribution-free ex post equilibrium may not exist; enter by giving each player a robust-optimization objective over a payoff uncertainty set (pp. 3, 8, 16).
key_idea: Replace the expectation in the best-response correspondence by an infimum over U; existence by Kakutani as in Nash; equilibria as a projection of a multilinear system obtained with the price-of-robustness LP-duality lemma (pp. 10, 16-25).
assumptions: Finite N-player one-shot simultaneous games; commonly known bounded uncertainty set (polyhedral for computation); no private information until Section 7, finite type spaces for computation there (pp. 4, 8, 18, 23, 40).
proof_devices: Worst-case expected payoff replaces expected payoff in the best response (p. 10); worst-case expected rather than expected worst-case payoff justified in footnote 4 (p. 11)
Existence via Kakutani: continuity of the worst-case expected payoff (Lemmas 2-3, p. 17) and concavity in own strategy (Lemma 4, p. 18); Theorem 2 (pp. 18-19)
Symmetric equilibria by restricting the best-response map to the diagonal (Theorem 5, pp. 33-34)
Infinite type spaces: Bohnenblust-Karlin fixed point in a Banach space of bounded functions (Theorems 7-8, pp. 38-40)
LP-duality lemma with extreme-point and constraint forms of a polyhedral uncertainty set (Lemma 5, pp. 21-22)
Double dualization of each player's robust LP gives the multilinear equilibrium system, with a size table (Theorem 3, pp. 23-25; Table 1, p. 25)
Sign-constant payoff sensitivities collapse the robust game to a nominal game with a worst-case payoff matrix (Theorem 4, pp. 28-29)
Quadratic penalty (Courant; Fiacco-McCormick) solved by a pseudo-Newton method with Armijo steps and random restarts (pp. 25-26)
Counterexample: an interval-cost inspection game has no ex post equilibrium (p. 16)
experiments: MATLAB 6.5 on a 1.7 GHz Pentium IV: inspection game solved in 0.5 s (71 iterations) to the predicted (0.4, 0.8); 15 restarts recover all 3 free-rider equilibria in 1.85 min; 10 network-routing instances (N<=5, a<=5), one 50-iteration run each, final penalty rising to 15.3 and relative error to 0.59; no baseline solver, no certificate beyond the penalty (pp. 26-28).
positioning: Extends Nash and Harsanyi (robust games named after Bayesian games); against the common prior (Morris, Wilson); separated from max-min ambiguity models on three counts (complete information, still probabilistic, no computation); RO lineage Soyster -> Ben-Tal-Nemirovski/El Ghaoui -> Bertsimas-Sim (robust LP stays LP) -> Bertsimas-Pachamanova-Sim (pp. 3, 5-8).
writing: Numbered contributions with a section map (pp. 3-5); two anticipated reader objections answered in their own subsections (pp. 12-14); economic intuition after each worked comparison (p. 31); closes on a modest hope (p. 41).
limits_future: Approximate penalty method with no convergence guarantee, small games only, larger routing instances end unsolved (pp. 26-28); computation needs finite type spaces (p. 40); no future directions (p. 41).

method_links.note: an equilibrium problem owned by game theory is rewritten as one robust LP per player and, through the price-of-robustness LP-duality lemma, as a finite multilinear system; a sign-monotone class maps to a nominal complete-information game so Nash-equilibrium methods apply; boundary printed (polyhedral U, finite type spaces)

title: Dynamic pricing: A learning approach
contribution: Jointly learns a linear demand curve and sets prices by dynamic programming with incomplete state information (exact 8-D, approximate 5-D, heuristic 1-D and myopic policies), and extends to duopoly with LP-based demand estimation and inverse optimization of the rival, tested in simulation (read: August 2001 manuscript).
problem_entry: {AP+SD+DA} Demand curves are unknown and must be learned while pricing a perishable product; revenue management mostly treats demand as an exogenous process with a given distribution and rarely models dynamics with competition (pp. 3-4).
key_idea: Estimate and price jointly in a DP whose state is compressed to the estimator's running sums; approximate and heuristic versions trade revenue for tractability; under competition, LP estimation of time-varying coefficients and inverse optimization of the rival (pp. 9-15, 26-29).
assumptions: Linear demand with Gaussian noise, one product, capacity given, costs ignored; 5-D DP freezes future noise variance; closed form only without noise; duopoly with slowly varying coefficients, sign constraints, rival assumed revenue-maximizing; synthetic data only (pp. 4, 6, 13, 18, 24-27).
proof_devices: Recursive least-squares update with explicit 2x2 inverse (Proposition 1, pp. 7-8)
Next-period variance forecast identifies the running sums the DP state must carry (Proposition 2, pp. 10-12)
Eight-dimensional DP with incomplete state information (p. 12); five-dimensional approximation freezing the future noise variance (pp. 13-14)
Averaging (exchange) argument: optimal deterministic prices are equal and unique (Lemma 1, pp. 16-18)
Three-case closed form for the deterministic price, clipped to the price interval (Theorem 2, pp. 18-19)
Equivalence of the 1-D and 5-D DPs without noise (pp. 19-20)
L1 regression with Lipschitz and sign constraints, transformable to an LP (p. 26)
Inverse optimization: fit the rival's demand parameters so its closed-form best price matches its observed prices (pp. 27-29)
experiments: Synthetic only. Monopoly (demand 60 - p + noise, c=400, T=20, 1,000 runs): 1-D DP beats myopic by 28.65% without noise; with noise (T=5, c=125) 1-D DP +9.4% over myopic and 5-D DP +2.09% over 1-D, 5-D with the largest variance; 8-D DP not implemented (pp. 21-23). Duopoly (T=150, uncapacitated, 1,000 runs): optimization-based pricing (with a last-price rival forecast, not the inverse-optimization one) beats random and matching except against an optimizing rival, where matching is slightly better; mirrored rows and an asymmetric symmetric pairing left unexplained (pp. 29-31). No run times or hardware.
positioning: Against revenue-management models with demand as an exogenous process and work ignoring dynamics plus competition (pp. 3-4); builds on Bertsekas's DP with incomplete state information (p. 9) and the authors' own time-varying regression with Gamarnik and Tsitsiklis (pp. 24-25); ten listed references never cited in the text (pp. 32-35).
writing: List-built introduction (problem characteristics, applications, contributions, pp. 3-5) and an Insights list (p. 24); hedged body, but abstract and conclusion claim gains whatever the rival does, beyond Table 3's near-tie (pp. 2, 30-31; Tension T6); draft traces: typos, no Theorem 1, promised open questions absent (pp. 5, 16-31).
limits_future: Exact 8-D DP intractable, tractable DPs approximate or heuristic (pp. 13-14, 21); competitive pricing myopic, tested uncapacitated with two firms (pp. 28-30); no learning guarantee for the joint scheme; open questions promised but not given (pp. 5, 31).

method_links.note: learning inside the decision: demand estimates carried in the DP state; policies scored by revenue (decision metric), not estimation error; joint estimation-and-pricing DPs beat the separated heuristic, which beats myopic pricing
no owner, partner data or current rule: synthetic linear demand; baselines are myopic, random and price-matching policies, whereas step 2 prefers the stronger naive rule

monopoly case stays inside dynamic programming and buys tractability by state compression and approximation, not by an LP/conic/MIO reformulation; only the competitive estimation is kept in the LP class; the 8-D DP boundary is printed

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Firm 1 assumes Firm 2 maximizes revenue and fits Firm 2's demand parameters so that Firm 2's closed-form optimal price reproduces its observed prices (uncapacitated and capacitated), under Lipschitz and sign constraints

transferable: Compress a learning DP: write the estimator's recursive update, list the running sums it needs, and make exactly those sums the state (pp. 7, 9-12).

Rank policies by computational intensity (myopic, certainty-equivalent 1-D DP, approximate 5-D DP, exact 8-D DP) and report the revenue each step buys on the same simulated instances (Tables 1-2, p. 23).
Fit time-varying demand coefficients by an L1 regression with Lipschitz and sign constraints, solved as an LP (p. 26).
Infer a competitor's demand parameters by assuming it optimizes and fitting its closed-form best response to its observed prices (pp. 27-29).
Solve the noiseless case in closed form (equal prices by an averaging argument; three-case proof) to explain what the DP policies do (pp. 16-19).

title: Tight bounds on expected order statistics
contribution: Computes tight bounds on the expected maximum of dependent random variables from means and variances (univariate convex problem solved by bisection) or covariances (SDP), with extremal distributions, closed-form bounds and improved bounds for general order statistics.
problem_entry: {CP+SD; AP application} Classical order-statistic bounds (Gumbel, Hartley-David, Arnold-Groeneveld, Aven) are not tight under general mean-variance information; define the tight bound as a sup over moment-feasible distributions (pp. 2-3).
key_idea: Majorize the maximum by a threshold plus the sum of positive parts, solve the univariate worst-case inner problem in closed form, show the thresholds coincide and reduce to a one-dimensional convex search; with covariances, the moment dual is an SDP (pp. 4-6, 10-11).
assumptions: Given means and variances (and a positive definite covariance matrix for the SDP case), no independence or distribution type; option example ignores price nonnegativity and assumes zero correlation (pp. 2-3, 11, 14, 16).
proof_devices: Threshold majorization of the maximum, then expectation and minimization (Theorem 1 sketch, p. 4)
Cauchy-Schwarz closed form for the worst-case E[(X-z)+] with a two-point extremal law (Proposition 1, p. 5)
Exchange argument: optimal thresholds coincide; strictly convex univariate problem and its first-order condition (Theorem 2, pp. 5-6)
Constructive tightness via an n-atom extremal distribution (Theorem 3, pp. 6-7)
Bisection with bracketing endpoints derived from the first-order condition; endpoints give closed-form bounds (pp. 8-9; Theorem 4, p. 9)
Moment-problem duality (Isii) plus the PSD representation of nonnegative quadratics gives an SDP (pp. 10-11)
Sum-of-top-order-statistics relaxation for k<n (eq. 23, p. 11; Theorems 5-6, p. 12)
experiments: Pentium II 550 MHz, under one minute in total. Lookback call on Andreasen's 10-period data, strikes 70-140: tight bound below Arnold-Groeneveld and Aven at every strike, equal to Boyle-Lin at the two highest strikes; covariance SDP (SeDuMi, zero correlation assumed) lowest (pp. 13-16). Simulation n=30, 100 random moment sets: mean errors vs the tight bound 7.73% and 108.93% (new closed forms), 22.86% (Arnold-Groeneveld), 16.91% (Aven) for the maximum; 14.21%, 1.04%, 3.13% for the second order statistic; weak variants reported (pp. 16-19).
positioning: Improves on Gumbel, Hartley-David, Arnold-Groeneveld and Aven (pp. 2-3); builds on Meilijson-Nadas and the authors' SIOPT 2004 paper (p. 4); extends Lai-Robbins/Ross from known marginals to known moments (p. 6); inner bound credited to Jagannathan and Scarf (p. 5), moment duality to Isii and Karlin-Studden (p. 10); option-bound lineage Lo, Bertsimas-Popescu, Boyle-Lin (p. 14).
writing: Numbered contributions mapped to sections (p. 3); tractability as the abstract's stated point (p. 1); hedged comparatives (pp. 3, 18); five-sentence summary with one open problem (p. 19).
limits_future: kth-order bounds not tight for k<n because the kth order statistic is not convex (p. 12); closed forms can lose to classical bounds in constructed cases (pp. 18-19); future: tight kth-order bounds under mean-variance and covariance information (p. 19).

method_links.note: a statistics question posed as optimization over distributions with given moments; reduced to a univariate convex problem (bisection) and an SDP; moment dual read and extremal distribution constructed; boundary printed (k<n not tight; open problem); tractability framed as polynomial-time SDP plus a named solver

duel-the-incumbent without MIO: the incumbent closed-form bounds (Arnold-Groeneveld, Aven, Boyle-Lin) are run on a published option example and on random moment data; the certificate is tightness through an extremal distribution, not a gap

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Subsume the incumbent as a special case
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: for identical means and variances the bisection bound reproduces Arnold-Groeneveld's bound exactly (k=n and general k); the result extends Lai-Robbins and Ross from known marginals to known moments

transferable: Tight bound by majorization, a univariate worst case and coinciding thresholds, finished by bisection (pp. 4-8).
Prove tightness constructively by building the extremal discrete distribution from the optimizer (pp. 6-7).
Turn the bracketing interval of a one-dimensional search into two closed-form bounds by evaluating the objective at its endpoints (pp. 8-9).
Test new bounds against every classical bound both on a published applied example and on random moment data, and report the error of the weak variant too (Tables 2-4, pp. 15-19).

quotes.text: Particularly, using optimization methods, we develop tractable approaches to compute bounds on the expected value of order statistics
Finding tight bounds for the general kth-order statistic under mean–variance and possibly covariance information is a potential research area for the future

title: Solving asymmetric variational inequalities via convex optimization
contribution: Reformulates asymmetric variational inequalities over polyhedral and conic sets, via LP and conic duality, as single-level smooth optimization problems that are convex under stated conditions (convex QPs for monotone affine VIs), with a duality-based MPEC extension.
problem_entry: {CP+LO; RO as the lens} Asymmetric-Jacobian VIs lack a single-level smooth reformulation that commercial solvers accept; merit functions are bilevel and at most once differentiable (pp. 2-3).
key_idea: x* solves the VI iff it optimizes the LP that F(x*) induces; dualize to get a single-level problem whose objective is the duality gap, convex under stated conditions; a VI is a robust constraint (pp. 3-7).
assumptions: K polyhedral in standard form or conic (strict feasibility for the converse); no existence assumed; convexity under concave F_j and convex F(x)'x; MPEC lower level varies only in its coefficients; no data (pp. 3-8).
proof_devices: Eaves's characterization: x* solves the VI iff it optimizes LP(x*); strong duality for necessity, weak duality for sufficiency (Theorem 1, pp. 3-4)
Duality gap as a nonnegative objective: zero certifies a solution, a positive value or infeasibility certifies none (Corollary 1 and Remark, p. 4)
Conic duality extension to general cones and the PSD cone (Theorem 2, Corollary 2, pp. 5-6)
Polynomial-size count (Table 1, p. 6) to certify complexity by reformulation (p. 6)
Sufficient convexity conditions; affine case reduces to monotonicity (Theorem 3, Corollary 3, p. 7)
One-dimensional counterexample F(x) = 1 - e^(-x): concave and monotone, F(x)x not convex (p. 7)
Symbolic Hessian eigenvalues in MAPLE to verify convexity (Example 3, p. 9)
Duality-based MPEC reformulation without complementarity constraints (Corollary 5, p. 8)
Equivalence with minimizing the classical primal gap function, lifted into a smooth higher-dimensional form (p. 9)
experiments: none (n/a): no computations; the practical claim rests on commercial-solver availability (pp. 2, 7).
positioning: Credits Eaves (p. 4) and RO's duality reformulations (p. 4); positioned against merit and regularized gap functions (Auchmuty, Fukushima) (pp. 2-3, 9) and the KKT-based MPEC reformulation of Luo-Pang-Ralph (p. 8); generalizes the complementarity-problem equivalence (p. 5).
writing: Letter format: three numbered contributions with section pointers (p. 3); practical-applicability argument from commercial solvers (p. 7); first-person hedges (pp. 2, 7); RO connection as a declared digression (p. 6).
limits_future: Convexity conditions only sufficient and fail as a test for monotone nonlinear F (p. 7); MPEC reformulation nonconvex when K(u) and F depend on u (p. 8); no numerical evidence; no future directions (p. 9).

method_links.note: VIs, owned by a community of specialized iterative algorithms, rewritten exactly as single-level smooth programs (convex LCQP for monotone affine F) so commercial solvers apply; duality gap as objective; boundary printed (sufficient conditions only, counterexample, nonconvex MPEC); tractable means polynomial-time certification here
the why-now is the availability and maturity of commercial convex solvers, argued qualitatively, with no measured figure or run time
weak: this paper and S029 come from one student's thesis (Aghassi 2005) carrying the RO programme into VIs and games; an alternative proof is deferred to the thesis

transferable: Self-referential optimality by LP duality: x* solves VI(K, F) iff min F(x*)'x over K equals F(x*)'x*; impose dual feasibility and a zero gap (pp. 3-4).
Use the duality gap itself as the objective: value zero certifies a solution, a positive value or infeasibility certifies there is none (p. 4).
Certify a problem's complexity by an exact, polynomial-size reformulation into a polynomially solvable class instead of designing a tailored algorithm (p. 6).
Kill a tempting sufficient condition with a one-dimensional counterexample (p. 7).
Show that a deprecated tool (the nonsmooth primal gap function) becomes smooth once lifted by duality into a slightly larger space (p. 9).

quotes.text: Namely, VI (1) is a robust constraint in which it is as if x is subject to uncertainty and known only to belong to K.

Since commercial optimization packages for single-level problems are available, supported, and refined through practice to a greater extent than are solvers specific to VIs, we believe that our reformulation has practical applicability.
